speaker_role: former admissions officer (self-described former admissions officer, incl. at Vanderbilt)
commercial_incentive: Yes, promotes his own newsletter and a paid 'parents ultimate course on college admissions' at askdrhoffman.com
key_insights: Explains demonstrated interest is tracked by colleges to predict yield (percent of admits who enroll), which matters to institutions.

Lists official tracked signals: campus visits/tours, email opens and click-throughs, website visit tracking ('pings'), and applying to/attending fly-in programs (roughly 75-80 US colleges offer these, mainly for underrepresented students).
States paid pre-college summer programs at a college's own campus are usually run by a separate office from admissions and typically only marginally affect admissions chances despite their cost.
Names American University, Tulane, and Lehigh as examples of schools known to weigh demonstrated interest.

Describes unofficial/informal signals that can leave impressions even at schools without formal DI tracking: thoughtful emails to a student's assigned regional admissions rep, questions at college fairs, attending high school visits, and sending thank-you notes.
Warns that excessive/overly frequent contact (e.g., near-daily emails) can create a negative impression despite being intended as a positive signal.
States applying Early Decision or Early Action is described as the strongest way to demonstrate interest, given ED's binding commitment.
Advises checking a college's Common Data Set section C7 ('basis for selection') for a 'level of applicant's interest' rating to see if a school formally weighs demonstrated interest.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker: about 75-80 US colleges offer fly-in programs
Speaker: Common Data Set section C7 lists 'level of applicants interest' as a rated selection factor for schools that disclose it
notable_or_distinctive: Gives a concrete, actionable method (Common Data Set section C7) for checking whether a specific college actually tracks demonstrated interest, plus a first-hand anecdote about over-emailing backfiring.
reliability_notes: Speaker's admissions-officer background and Vanderbilt anecdote are self-reported and unverifiable; ends with a pitch for a paid course, so some depth is withheld to drive signups.
